case: A 34-year-old man is admitted to the burn unit after a house fire with full-thickness and partial-thickness burns covering 45% of his total body surface area. He required large-volume fluid resuscitation for hypotension during the first 24 hours. On hospital day 4, he vomits blood and passes black stools. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Hemoglobin has fallen from 14.1 g/dL to 9.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5). Upper endoscopy shows multiple shallow erosions in the gastric body and a 1.5-cm ulcer on the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb. Diagnosis: Curling ulcer (acute stress ulceration) after severe burns.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most important mechanism of mucosal injury in this patient?
options: Reduced prostaglandin synthesis from cyclooxygenase-1 inhibition
Urease-producing bacterial colonization of the antral mucosa
Mucosal ischemia from hypovolemia and splanchnic constriction
Vagally mediated increase in parietal cell acid output
approach: Note the setting: a severe burn with hypotension, and ulcers that appear within days.
Recall that Curling ulcers follow burns, while Cushing ulcers follow brain injury.
Link burn shock to low splanchnic blood flow, which weakens the mucosal barrier.
questions.why: After a major burn, plasma is lost from the circulation and the body shunts blood away from the gut. Low mucosal blood flow cuts the supply of oxygen and bicarbonate to the epithelium, slows cell renewal, and weakens the mucus and bicarbonate barrier. Even normal amounts of acid can then damage the mucosa and produce multiple acute erosions and ulcers within days. Curling ulcers are classically described in the proximal duodenum.
whyNot: Loss of protective prostaglandins from cyclooxygenase-1 inhibition is how NSAIDs injure the mucosa. Nothing in his history points to NSAID use.
Helicobacter pylori causes chronic antral gastritis and most ordinary duodenal ulcers over months to years. It does not explain ulcers that appear within days of a burn.
Correct.
Vagal overstimulation that raises acid output is the mechanism of a Cushing ulcer, which follows head injury or raised intracranial pressure. This patient had burns and shock, with no brain injury.

questions.stem: On hospital day 6, he develops brisk hematemesis and his blood pressure falls to 78/40 mm Hg. Repeat endoscopy shows a visible vessel spurting from the base of the posterior duodenal bulb ulcer. Which of the following arteries is most likely bleeding?
options: Gastroduodenal artery
Left gastric artery
Splenic artery
Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery
approach: Locate the ulcer: posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.
Recall which artery runs directly behind the duodenal bulb.
The gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, lies there.
questions.why: The celiac trunk gives off the common hepatic artery, which gives off the gastroduodenal artery. This vessel descends directly behind the first part of the duodenum before dividing into the right gastroepiploic and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries. An ulcer that penetrates the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb can erode it and cause life-threatening bleeding. Anterior duodenal ulcers tend to perforate into the peritoneal cavity instead.
whyNot: Correct.
The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach. It is the usual source of bleeding from a lesser curvature gastric ulcer.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas behind the stomach. A posterior gastric ulcer can erode it, but it does not lie behind the duodenal bulb.
The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery comes from the superior mesenteric artery and supplies the lower duodenum and pancreatic head. It does not run behind the first part of the duodenum.

questions.stem: After the bleeding is controlled, enteral feeding with a peptide-based formula is started through a nasogastric tube. Gastric acid output rises during the feeding. Which of the following best explains the effect of the peptides on acid secretion?
options: Stimulation of antral D cells to release somatostatin
Stimulation of duodenal S cells to release secretin
Stimulation of duodenal I cells to release cholecystokinin
Stimulation of antral G cells to release gastrin
approach: Identify the phase: food in the stomach means the gastric phase.
Recall that peptides and amino acids in the antrum are a direct stimulus for G cells.
Follow gastrin to histamine release and parietal cell activation.
questions.why: In the gastric phase, which produces most of the acid in a meal, peptides and amino acids in the antrum stimulate G cells to release gastrin into the blood. Gastrin acts mainly on enterochromaffin-like cells, which release histamine onto nearby parietal cells, and it also stimulates parietal cells directly. Gastric distension adds vagovagal and local cholinergic reflexes. All of these signals converge on the H+/K+ ATPase, the final step that pumps acid into the lumen.
whyNot: Somatostatin from D cells inhibits gastrin release and parietal cell secretion. D cells are stimulated mainly by acid in the lumen, which acts as a brake on secretion.
Secretin is released when acid enters the duodenum. It stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate and inhibits gastrin release, so it lowers gastric acid output.

Cholecystokinin is released by fats and amino acids in the duodenum. It stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzymes and slows gastric emptying, and its overall effect on acid secretion is inhibitory.
Correct.

questions.stem: Biopsies taken from the gastric body during endoscopy show intact oxyntic glands. If these glands were instead destroyed by autoimmune gastritis, which of the following sets of findings would be expected?
options: Low acid, low intrinsic factor, low gastrin
Low acid, low intrinsic factor, high gastrin
Low acid, normal intrinsic factor, low gastrin
High acid, low intrinsic factor, high gastrin
approach: Recall that oxyntic glands of the body and fundus hold parietal and chief cells.
Parietal cells make both HCl and intrinsic factor, so both fall when they are destroyed.
The antrum is spared, and loss of acid removes somatostatin braking, so gastrin rises.
questions.why: Autoimmune gastritis targets parietal cells and intrinsic factor in the body and fundus. Losing parietal cells removes both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which leads to achlorhydria and, over years, vitamin B12 deficiency. Chief cells are also lost, so pepsinogen I falls. The antral G cells are spared, and without acid to trigger somatostatin release, gastrin climbs high and drives enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia.
whyNot: The antral G cells are spared in autoimmune gastritis. Without acid to stimulate somatostatin release, gastrin rises.
Correct.
Intrinsic factor comes from the same parietal cells that make acid, so it falls along with acid. Gastrin rises, since the antral G cells are spared and lose acid feedback.
Acid comes from parietal cells, which are destroyed. High acid with high gastrin is the pattern of a gastrin-secreting tumor (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).

dx: Reflux esophagitis with a sliding hiatal hernia in pregnancy
case: A 31-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of burning retrosternal pain after meals and when lying down, sour regurgitation at night, and pain with swallowing. Her symptoms began at about 20 weeks' gestation and have worsened. Her body mass index before pregnancy was 31 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits, and the fetal heart rate is normal. Because of persistent odynophagia, upper endoscopy is performed. It shows a 3-cm sliding hiatal hernia and several linear erosions in the distal 5 cm of the esophagus. Diagnosis: reflux esophagitis with a sliding hiatal hernia during pregnancy.

questions.stem: In addition to her hiatal hernia and higher intra-abdominal pressure, which of the following most directly contributes to her reflux?
options: Increased vagal cholinergic tone to the LES muscle
Progesterone-mediated decrease in LES resting tone
Estrogen-mediated increase in parietal cell acid output
Motilin-mediated increase in migrating motor complexes
approach: Identify the risk factors named: pregnancy, obesity, and hiatal hernia.
Recall that progesterone relaxes smooth muscle throughout the gut.
Apply it to the lower esophageal sphincter: lower resting tone lets acid reflux.
questions.why: Reflux happens when the antireflux barrier fails through transient sphincter relaxations, a low resting sphincter pressure, or a hiatal hernia. In pregnancy, rising progesterone relaxes the smooth muscle of the lower esophageal sphincter and lowers its resting pressure. The enlarging uterus raises intra-abdominal pressure and pushes gastric contents upward. Her obesity and sliding hernia add to the same problem, which is why symptoms worsen as pregnancy advances.
whyNot: Vagal cholinergic input contracts the lower esophageal sphincter and raises its tone. More of it would protect against reflux.
Correct.
Pregnancy hormones do not meaningfully raise gastric acid output. Reflux in pregnancy comes from a weak barrier at the gastroesophageal junction.
Migrating motor complexes sweep the fasting gut clean and would speed clearance. Progesterone tends to slow gut motility.

topics: Hormonal effects on gut smooth muscle

questions.stem: Biopsies are taken from the mid and distal esophagus. Which of the following findings would most strongly support reflux esophagitis over eosinophilic esophagitis?
options: Dense eosinophils, 15 or more per high-power field, in mid and distal biopsies
Concentric mucosal rings and linear furrows along the esophageal length
A sharply punched-out ulcer in the mid esophagus near the aortic arch
Scattered eosinophils, under 15 per high-power field, in distal biopsies only
approach: Recall that both conditions can show eosinophils and basal cell hyperplasia.
Separate them by eosinophil count and by where they are found.
Reflux injures the distal esophagus most, with only a few eosinophils.
questions.why: Acid reflux injures the squamous epithelium closest to the stomach. Biopsies show basal zone hyperplasia, elongated lamina propria papillae, and a few intraepithelial eosinophils and neutrophils, mostly in the distal esophagus. Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergic, Th2-driven disease with dense eosinophils (15 or more per high-power field) along the whole esophagus. A normal mid-esophageal biopsy with mild distal changes points to reflux.
whyNot: Fifteen or more eosinophils per high-power field in both the mid and distal esophagus is the histologic definition of eosinophilic esophagitis, often in a patient with atopy and food impaction.
Stacked rings (trachealization) and linear furrows are the classic endoscopic look of eosinophilic esophagitis.
A discrete mid-esophageal ulcer where the aortic arch narrows the lumen suggests pill esophagitis, from a tablet such as doxycycline lodging there.
Correct.

questions.stem: In her type of hiatal hernia, which part of the stomach is displaced into the thorax together with the gastroesophageal junction?
options: Cardia
Fundus
Antrum
Pylorus
approach: Define a sliding hernia: the gastroesophageal junction moves up through the hiatus.
Name the stomach region that surrounds the gastroesophageal junction.
That region, the cardia, goes up with it.
questions.why: The stomach has five regions: cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and pylorus. The cardia is the small zone that surrounds the opening of the esophagus. In a sliding hiatal hernia, the most common type, the gastroesophageal junction and cardia slide up through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax. This removes the help that the crura normally give the sphincter and favors reflux. In a paraesophageal hernia, the junction stays put and the fundus herniates beside the esophagus.
whyNot: Correct.
The fundus rolls up beside an esophagus that stays in place in a paraesophageal (rolling) hernia. In a sliding hernia the junction itself moves up.
The antrum is the distal stomach near the pylorus. It is not displaced in a small sliding hernia.
The pylorus is the outlet to the duodenum, far from the hiatus. It stays in the abdomen.

questions.stem: Refluxed acid is normally cleared from her esophagus by secondary peristalsis triggered by distension. Which of the following best describes how the enteric nervous system propels the bolus?
options: Simultaneous contraction of the whole length of the esophageal body
Motilin-driven contraction that moves from the distal to the proximal end
Cholinergic contraction above and nitrergic relaxation below the bolus
Nitrergic relaxation above and cholinergic contraction below the bolus
approach: Recall the law of the intestine: contract behind the bolus, relax in front of it.
Name the transmitters: acetylcholine and substance P contract, nitric oxide and VIP relax.
Match the option with the right transmitter on the right side.
questions.why: Peristalsis is coordinated by the myenteric plexus. When a bolus stretches the wall, excitatory neurons release acetylcholine and substance P to contract the circular muscle on the oral side. Inhibitory neurons release nitric oxide and VIP to relax the muscle on the anal side. The ring of contraction moves down the tube and pushes the bolus ahead of it. Secondary peristalsis uses this local reflex to clear refluxed acid back into the stomach.
whyNot: Simultaneous contractions do not propel anything. This is the abnormal pattern of distal esophageal spasm.
Motilin drives the fasting migrating motor complex in the stomach and small bowel, and it moves in the oral to anal direction.
Correct.
This pattern would push the bolus backward toward the mouth. The contraction must be behind the bolus.

case: A 24-year-old man with ulcerative colitis diagnosed 3 years ago is brought to the emergency department because of 10 days of bloody diarrhea, 12 stools daily, and 2 days of increasing abdominal swelling and pain. He stopped his maintenance medication 2 months ago. Temperature is 39.0 °C (102.2 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. The abdomen is distended and diffusely tender with reduced bowel sounds. Leukocyte count is 16,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). An abdominal x-ray shows the transverse colon dilated to 8 cm (normal under 6 cm). Diagnosis: ulcerative colitis complicated by toxic megacolon.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings was most likely seen on colonoscopic biopsy when his disease was first diagnosed?
options: Skip lesions with transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas
Caseating granulomas with ulcers clustered in the ileocecal region
Flask-shaped ulcers with trophozoites that contain ingested red cells
Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum with crypt abscesses
approach: Recall the distribution of ulcerative colitis: rectum first, then continuous proximal spread.
Recall its depth: mucosa and submucosa only.
Match the histology: neutrophils in crypts form crypt abscesses.
questions.why: Ulcerative colitis always involves the rectum and extends proximally in one continuous stretch. Inflammation is limited to the mucosa and submucosa. Neutrophils invade crypts to form crypt abscesses, and chronic disease distorts crypt architecture. Ulcers undermine the mucosa, and islands of regenerating mucosa between them form pseudopolyps. Granulomas and skip lesions argue for Crohn disease.
whyNot: Skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and noncaseating granulomas are the pattern of Crohn disease.
Caseating granulomas in the ileocecal region suggest intestinal tuberculosis.
Flask-shaped ulcers with trophozoites that ingest red cells are typical of amebic colitis from Entamoeba histolytica.
Correct.

questions.stem: He recovers after medical treatment. Which of the following long-term complications is more characteristic of his disease than of Crohn disease?
options: Vitamin B12 deficiency
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis
Enterocutaneous fistula
approach: Sort complications by mechanism: transmural or ileal disease points to Crohn disease.
Recall which extraintestinal problem is linked most strongly to ulcerative colitis.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis fits; it occurs in a large share of patients with ulcerative colitis.
questions.why: Most patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis have inflammatory bowel disease, usually ulcerative colitis. The bile ducts become inflamed and fibrosed, giving a beaded pattern on cholangiography, a cholestatic rise in alkaline phosphatase, and p-ANCA positivity in many cases. It raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma and of colorectal cancer. Fistulas, strictures, B12 deficiency, and oxalate stones all come from transmural or ileal disease in Crohn disease.
whyNot: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum, which is often diseased or resected in Crohn disease. Ulcerative colitis spares the small bowel, apart from mild backwash ileitis.
Correct.
Oxalate stones follow fat malabsorption in ileal Crohn disease. Unabsorbed fat binds calcium, which frees oxalate to be absorbed in the colon.
Fistulas need transmural inflammation, which is a feature of Crohn disease. Ulcerative colitis stays in the mucosa.

questions.stem: His younger brother has Crohn disease of the terminal ileum and carries a loss-of-function NOD2 variant. Which of the following best explains how this variant predisposes to Crohn disease?
options: Loss of FOXP3 expression in regulatory T cells
Deficient transport of secretory IgA across the epithelium
Impaired cytosolic sensing of bacterial peptidoglycan
Excess binding of bacterial lipopolysaccharide by surface TLR4
approach: Recall that NOD2 is an intracellular pattern recognition receptor.
Name its ligand: muramyl dipeptide from bacterial peptidoglycan.
Link weak sensing to poor clearance of commensal bacteria and a chronic Th1 and Th17 response.
questions.why: NOD2 is a cytosolic receptor in Paneth cells, monocytes, and macrophages that recognizes muramyl dipeptide from bacterial peptidoglycan. Loss-of-function variants weaken antimicrobial defensin release and bacterial killing, so commensal bacteria cross the epithelium and persist. The immune system answers with an exaggerated Th1 response (interferon-gamma) and Th17 response (IL-17) that drives transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Crohn disease often affects the terminal ileum, where Paneth cells are most dense.
whyNot: FOXP3 mutations cause IPEX syndrome, with severe enteropathy, type 1 diabetes, and dermatitis in infant boys. They are not the NOD2 mechanism.
Secretory IgA is carried across the epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor. NOD2 is an innate sensor inside the cell and has no role in IgA transport.
Correct.
Toll-like receptor 4 senses lipopolysaccharide at the cell surface. NOD2 is a separate, cytosolic receptor, and the Crohn variants reduce its function.

topics: Th1 and Th17 in Crohn disease

questions.stem: Two years later he has a total colectomy with an end ileostomy. Over the next several months, the ileostomy output averages 2 L/day. He then develops poor healing of the stoma site, reduced taste, and scaly, red plaques around the mouth and on the hands. Deficiency of which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Zinc
Copper
Iron
Selenium
approach: Note the cause: large, ongoing intestinal fluid losses.
Group the findings: poor wound healing, dysgeusia, and periorificial and acral dermatitis.
Match the triad to the mineral lost in intestinal fluid.
questions.why: Zinc is lost in large amounts in diarrhea and high-output stomas. It is a cofactor for many enzymes, including those needed for cell division, collagen formation, and taste. Deficiency causes poor wound healing, loss of taste and smell, hair loss, and a scaly, red dermatitis around the mouth, anus, and on the hands and feet, called acrodermatitis. The inherited form, acrodermatitis enteropathica, comes from a defect in intestinal zinc uptake.
whyNot: Correct.
Copper deficiency causes anemia, neutropenia, and a myelopathy that resembles vitamin B12 deficiency. It does not cause this rash or taste loss.
Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia, fatigue, glossitis, and spoon-shaped nails. It does not cause periorificial dermatitis.
Selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and muscle weakness. Skin and taste changes are not its pattern.

dx: Internal hemorrhoids with a coexisting anal fissure
case: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician 3 months after a vaginal delivery because of bright red blood on the toilet paper after bowel movements and a soft swelling that protrudes from the anus during defecation and reduces spontaneously. She has had constipation with hard stools since late pregnancy. For the past 3 weeks, she has also had sharp, tearing pain during defecation that lasts for an hour afterward. Vital signs are within normal limits. Inspection shows a small linear tear in the posterior midline of the anoderm. Anoscopy shows engorged vascular cushions above the pectinate line. Diagnosis: grade II internal hemorrhoids with an acute anal fissure.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the development of her hemorrhoids?
options: Straining that engorges and displaces the anal vascular cushions
Portal hypertension diverting blood through rectal portosystemic anastomoses
Obstruction and infection of the anal glands at the pectinate line
Weakness of the pelvic floor allowing full-thickness rectal descent
approach: Note her risks: constipation, straining, and recent pregnancy.
Recall that hemorrhoids are normal vascular cushions that become enlarged and slide down.
Choose the mechanism that links straining to cushion engorgement.
questions.why: Everyone has anal cushions, made of submucosal vessels and connective tissue that help seal the anal canal. Straining with hard stools and the pressure of a pregnant uterus on pelvic veins engorge these cushions, and their supporting tissue stretches so they slide downward. Internal hemorrhoids arise above the pectinate line. They cause painless bright red bleeding and may prolapse; grade II hemorrhoids return on their own. External hemorrhoids lie below the line and hurt when they thrombose.
whyNot: Correct.
Portal hypertension opens anorectal varices at the portosystemic anastomosis, which are a different lesion from hemorrhoids. She has no liver disease.
Obstructed, infected anal glands produce an anorectal abscess, which causes constant throbbing pain and fever.
Full-thickness descent of the rectal wall through the anus is rectal prolapse, which shows concentric mucosal folds. Her swelling is engorged vascular cushions.

questions.stem: Her hemorrhoids are painless, but her fissure is very painful. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Sympathetic afferents above the pectinate line and vagal afferents below
Absent sensory fibers above the pectinate line and pelvic splanchnic fibers below
Visceral afferents above the pectinate line and pudendal somatic fibers below
Pudendal somatic fibers above the pectinate line and visceral afferents below
approach: Locate each lesion: internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line, fissure below it.
Recall that the area above the line is endoderm-derived gut with visceral innervation.
The area below is ectoderm-derived skin supplied by the inferior rectal branches of the pudendal nerve.
questions.why: The pectinate line marks where gut endoderm meets ectoderm. Above it, the mucosa has visceral innervation that senses stretch but not cutting or tearing, so internal hemorrhoids are painless. Below it, the anoderm is supplied by somatic fibers in the inferior rectal nerve, a branch of the pudendal nerve, so a fissure there is sharply painful. The same line divides the epithelium, the arterial supply, portal versus systemic venous drainage, and internal iliac versus superficial inguinal lymph drainage.
whyNot: The vagus does not supply the anal canal. Visceral fibers above the line travel with the pelvic splanchnic and inferior hypogastric nerves, and the area below is somatic.
The mucosa above the line does have visceral afferents that sense stretch, and pelvic splanchnic nerves carry visceral fibers.
Correct.
This reverses the anatomy. The pudendal nerve supplies the skin-lined anal canal below the line.

questions.stem: Eight months later, she returns because of 2 days of constant, throbbing perianal pain that is worse when sitting. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). There is a tender, red, fluctuant swelling beside the anal verge. Which of the following is the most likely origin of this new problem?
options: Extension of the posterior fissure into the rectal wall
Infected, obstructed anal glands at the pectinate line
Thrombosis within the inferior rectal venous plexus
Strangulation of a prolapsed, irreducible internal hemorrhoid
approach: Note the new features: fever, constant pain, and a fluctuant swelling.
Recognize an anorectal abscess.
Recall that most begin in anal glands that open into the crypts at the pectinate line.
questions.why: Anal glands open into the anal crypts at the pectinate line. When a gland duct becomes blocked, bacteria multiply and form an abscess that spreads into the perianal or ischioanal tissues. The result is constant throbbing pain, fever, and a tender fluctuant swelling. After drainage, many abscesses leave a fistula between the crypt and the perianal skin. Recurrent abscesses and fistulas should raise concern for Crohn disease.
whyNot: Fissures stay in the anoderm below the pectinate line. A fissure does not track into the rectum to form a fluctuant mass.
Correct.
A thrombosed external hemorrhoid is a painful, bluish, firm lump at the anal verge. It does not cause fever or fluctuance.
A strangulated internal hemorrhoid is a painful, dark, irreducible mass protruding through the anus. It is not a fluctuant collection beside the anus.

questions.stem: Her delivery was prolonged, with forceps assistance. Stretch injury to both pudendal nerves during such a delivery would most directly impair which of the following components of fecal continence?
options: Reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter to rectal filling
Resting tone of the internal anal sphincter between defecations
Rectal stretch sensation carried by pelvic splanchnic afferents
Voluntary contraction of the external anal sphincter
approach: List the parts of continence: rectal sensation, internal sphincter reflex, and external sphincter control.
Recall which nerve supplies each part.
The pudendal nerve supplies the voluntary external sphincter, so its loss causes urge incontinence.
questions.why: When stool enters the rectum, stretch receptors signal fullness and the internal anal sphincter relaxes by a reflex through the myenteric plexus. Continence then depends on voluntary contraction of the external anal sphincter and puborectalis, which are skeletal muscles supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4). Pudendal injury from a prolonged or instrumented delivery weakens this voluntary squeeze. The person feels the urge but cannot hold stool until she reaches a toilet.
whyNot: Reflex relaxation of the internal sphincter when the rectum fills is mediated by the myenteric plexus in the gut wall. It survives pudendal injury.
The internal sphincter is smooth muscle with tone maintained by its own properties and autonomic input. The pudendal nerve does not supply it.
Stretch of the rectum is sensed by visceral afferents traveling with the pelvic splanchnic nerves. These are separate from the pudendal nerve.
Correct.

dx: Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula and duodenal atresia in trisomy 21
case: A newborn girl born at 37 weeks' gestation is noted to have frothy oral secretions, and she chokes, coughs, and becomes cyanotic at her first feed. The pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios. She has upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, and single transverse palmar creases. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed beyond 10 cm, and a chest x-ray shows it coiled in a blind upper esophageal pouch. An abdominal x-ray shows two large gas-filled bubbles in the upper abdomen with no gas beyond them. Karyotype is 47,XX,+21. Diagnosis: esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula and duodenal atresia in a newborn with trisomy 21.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the presence of gas in her stomach?
options: Swallowed air passes through a narrowed but open esophagus
Bacteria in the stomach produce gas by fermenting milk
A fistula joins the trachea to the distal esophagus
A fistula joins the trachea to the proximal esophageal pouch
approach: Note the blind upper pouch: swallowed air cannot reach the stomach that way.
Ask how air enters the stomach anyway: through the airway.
A fistula from the trachea to the lower esophagus carries inspired air into the stomach.
questions.why: The most common type of esophageal atresia, about 85% of cases, has a blind upper pouch and a fistula from the trachea to the distal esophagus. Each breath and cry pushes air through the fistula into the stomach, so the abdomen contains gas. Saliva fills the blind pouch and spills into the larynx, causing drooling, choking, and cyanosis with feeds. The fetus could not swallow amniotic fluid, which caused polyhydramnios. Look for VACTERL anomalies: vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb defects.
whyNot: The case states the esophagus ends in a blind pouch, so no air can pass from the upper esophagus to the stomach.
The newborn gut has very few bacteria, and she has not been fed successfully. Fermentation does not explain gas within the first hours of life.
Correct.
A fistula from the trachea to the upper pouch can send saliva into the lungs. Without a distal connection, air could not reach the stomach, and the abdomen would be gasless.

questions.stem: Abnormal development of which of the following structures most likely produced her esophageal defect?
options: Urorectal septum
Pleuroperitoneal membrane
Aorticopulmonary septum
Tracheoesophageal septum
approach: Recognize the lesion as a faulty separation of the foregut into trachea and esophagus.
Recall that the respiratory diverticulum grows from the ventral foregut in week 4.
The tracheoesophageal septum divides the two; when it deviates or fails, atresia and fistula result.
questions.why: In week 4, the respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral wall of the foregut. Tracheoesophageal ridges grow toward each other and fuse into the tracheoesophageal septum, which separates the ventral trachea from the dorsal esophagus. If the septum deviates posteriorly or the division is incomplete, the esophagus may end blindly and a channel may remain between the trachea and esophagus. These defects often occur with other VACTERL anomalies.
whyNot: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the rectum and urogenital sinus. Defects cause anorectal malformations and fistulas to the urinary tract.
Failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to close leaves a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, usually on the left, with bowel in the chest.
The aorticopulmonary septum divides the truncus arteriosus. Its defects cause persistent truncus arteriosus or transposition of the great arteries.
Correct.

questions.stem: At surgery, the second part of the duodenum ends blindly just distal to the major duodenal papilla, with no pancreatic tissue around it. Failure of which of the following developmental processes most likely explains this finding?
options: Recanalization of the solid-stage duodenal lumen
Migration of the ventral pancreatic bud around the duodenum
Counterclockwise rotation of the midgut around the SMA
Obliteration of the vitelline duct at the ileum
approach: Note the findings: a blind-ending duodenum with a double bubble and no distal gas.
Recall that the duodenal lumen fills with cells in weeks 5 to 6 and opens again by about the end of week 8.
Failed reopening leaves atresia, which is strongly linked to Down syndrome.
questions.why: Epithelial cells briefly fill the lumen of the duodenum during weeks 5 to 6. The lumen normally reopens by vacuolization by about the end of the second month. If this recanalization fails, the duodenum is blocked, usually near or just beyond the major papilla, so vomitus contains bile. The stomach and proximal duodenum fill with gas to make the double bubble sign, and the fetus cannot absorb swallowed fluid, adding to polyhydramnios. About a quarter to a third of infants with duodenal atresia have Down syndrome.
whyNot: Correct.
Abnormal migration of the ventral pancreatic bud forms an annular pancreas, a ring of pancreas around the duodenum. The case states there is no pancreatic tissue around the obstruction.
Malrotation leaves the cecum high and allows Ladd bands or volvulus to compress the duodenum. It does not create a blind-ending duodenum.
A persistent vitelline duct remnant forms a Meckel diverticulum in the ileum. It does not cause duodenal obstruction at birth.

questions.stem: Saliva pools in her blind upper pouch. In a healthy newborn, once a bolus of milk reaches the pharynx, which of the following controls its passage into the esophagus?
options: Sympathetic outflow from the thoracic spinal cord
Reflex program of the medullary swallowing center
Voluntary commands from the primary motor cortex
Local myenteric reflexes independent of the brainstem
approach: Divide swallowing into oral, pharyngeal, and esophageal phases.
Recall that only the oral phase is voluntary.
The pharyngeal phase is a reflex run by the medullary swallowing center.
questions.why: Swallowing begins voluntarily when the tongue pushes the bolus back. Contact with the pharynx triggers a fixed reflex sequence controlled by the swallowing center in the medulla. The soft palate seals the nasopharynx, the larynx rises and the epiglottis covers it, breathing stops briefly, and the upper esophageal sphincter relaxes. Primary peristalsis then carries the bolus down, and vagal inhibitory nerves relax the lower esophageal sphincter ahead of it.
whyNot: Sympathetic outflow does not drive swallowing. The pharyngeal phase uses cranial nerves IX, X, and the nucleus ambiguus.
Correct.
Only the oral phase of swallowing is voluntary. Once the bolus touches the pharynx, the sequence cannot be stopped by will.
The pharynx and upper esophagus are skeletal muscle controlled by brainstem motor nuclei. The myenteric plexus governs the smooth muscle of the lower esophagus.

case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 5 months of progressive difficulty swallowing solid food, with a sensation that food sticks in her throat. She also reports fatigue. She had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 8 years ago and stopped taking supplements 3 years ago. Physical examination shows pallor, a smooth red tongue, cracks at the corners of the mouth, and spoon-shaped fingernails. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), mean corpuscular volume is 68 fL (80 to 100), and ferritin is 5 ng/mL (15 to 150). A barium swallow shows a thin shelf-like membrane in the upper esophagus just below the cricopharyngeus. Diagnosis: Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

questions.stem: This patient has an increased long-term risk of which of the following?
options: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the stomach
Squamous cell carcinoma of the upper esophagus
Adenocarcinoma arising in Barrett esophagus
Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the stomach
approach: Identify the lesion: an upper esophageal web with iron deficiency anemia.
Recall the cancer linked to Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
Contrast it with the lower esophageal Schatzki ring, a benign ring at the squamocolumnar junction.
questions.why: Plummer-Vinson syndrome combines iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and webs in the upper esophagus. Webs are thin mucosal folds that cause dysphagia mainly for solids. The syndrome carries a higher risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the hypopharynx and upper esophagus, so patients need follow-up. A Schatzki ring is a different lesion in the lower esophagus at the squamocolumnar junction that causes intermittent solid food dysphagia, often with a hiatal hernia.
whyNot: A gastrointestinal stromal tumor arises from interstitial cells of Cajal, usually with a KIT mutation. It has no link to iron deficiency or webs.
Correct.
Distal esophageal adenocarcinoma arises from Barrett metaplasia after long-standing reflux. A Schatzki ring sits at that level but carries no comparable cancer risk.
Gastric MALT lymphoma (extranodal marginal zone lymphoma) is driven by chronic Helicobacter pylori infection. It is not linked to esophageal webs.

questions.stem: She is treated with intravenous iron. Six months later, her ferritin is normal, but hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with an absolute neutrophil count of 900/mm3 (1,500 to 8,000). She has a new unsteady gait with loss of vibration and position sense in the feet. She has been taking a high-dose zinc supplement daily since her treatment began. Serum vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid levels are normal. Deficiency of which of the following most likely explains these new findings?
options: Copper
Vitamin B12
Folate
Vitamin E
approach: Group the findings: anemia, neutropenia, and a dorsal column myelopathy.
B12 deficiency looks similar, but her B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal.
Link high zinc intake and gastric bypass to copper deficiency.
questions.why: Copper deficiency produces anemia, neutropenia, and a myelopathy that closely mimics subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency. Two of her risks point there. Gastric bypass bypasses the stomach and proximal small bowel, where copper is absorbed. High zinc intake induces metallothionein in enterocytes, which binds copper tightly so it is lost when the cells shed into the lumen. Stopping zinc and replacing copper corrects the blood counts, though nerve damage may not fully recover.
whyNot: Correct.
Vitamin B12 deficiency also causes anemia, neutropenia, and dorsal column myelopathy, but her normal B12 and methylmalonic acid levels rule it out.
Folate deficiency causes a megaloblastic anemia but no myelopathy.
Vitamin E deficiency causes spinocerebellar degeneration and hemolytic anemia. It does not cause neutropenia, and it is not linked to zinc excess.

questions.stem: Biopsy of the web would most likely show which of the following lining epithelia?
options: Keratinized stratified squamous
Simple columnar with interspersed goblet cells
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous
approach: Locate the web: the upper esophagus.
Recall that a web is a fold of mucosa, covered by the normal local epithelium.
The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
questions.why: An esophageal web is a thin fold of mucosa that projects into the lumen, so it is covered by the normal esophageal lining: nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium over lamina propria. This lining resists abrasion from swallowed food. The stomach and intestine are lined by simple columnar epithelium. At the gastroesophageal junction, chronic acid reflux can replace squamous cells with columnar cells and goblet cells, which is Barrett metaplasia and the precursor of adenocarcinoma.
whyNot: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium covers the skin. The esophagus is normally nonkeratinized.
Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells is intestinal metaplasia, the change of Barrett esophagus in the distal esophagus.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the trachea and bronchi.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her bypass routes food from a small gastric pouch directly into the jejunum. Diversion of food away from which of the following segments most directly explains her original anemia?
options: Terminal ileum
Ascending colon
Duodenum
Distal jejunum
approach: Identify the anemia: microcytic with very low ferritin, so iron deficiency.
Recall where iron is absorbed: mostly the duodenum and proximal jejunum.
Note that the Roux-en-Y bypass diverts food past the duodenum.
questions.why: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum. There, acid helps keep it soluble, duodenal cytochrome b reduces ferric to ferrous iron, and DMT1 carries it into enterocytes. A Roux-en-Y gastric bypass sends food from a small gastric pouch straight into the jejunum, skipping the duodenum. The small pouch also makes little acid. Folate is absorbed in the jejunum, and B12 and bile acids in the terminal ileum.
whyNot: The terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile acids. Loss of it would cause a macrocytic anemia, and it still receives food after this operation.
The colon absorbs water and electrolytes and very little iron.
Correct.
The distal jejunum continues to receive food after a Roux-en-Y bypass. It is not the main site of iron uptake.

case: A 4-week-old boy, his parents' first child, is brought to the physician because of forceful vomiting after every feed for 5 days. The vomitus is milk without green or yellow staining, and he is eager to feed again right after vomiting. He was born at term and fed well until 3 weeks of age. At 2 weeks, he received a course of oral erythromycin after a pertussis exposure. He weighs less than he did at birth. His mucous membranes are dry. A firm, mobile, olive-sized mass is felt in the epigastrium. Ultrasonography shows pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm (normal under 3 mm). Diagnosis: infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his vomiting began at 3 weeks of age rather than at birth?
options: Postnatal hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle
Delayed failure of recanalization of the pyloric lumen
Gradual twisting of the midgut around the mesenteric root
Progressive scarring after an ulcer in the pyloric channel
approach: Note the timing: normal feeding, then onset at 2 to 6 weeks.
Recall that the pylorus is open at birth and the muscle thickens over the first weeks.
Choose the option that develops after birth and makes a palpable mass.
questions.why: In infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, the circular smooth muscle of the pylorus thickens after birth. The channel gradually narrows until milk cannot leave the stomach, which usually happens between 2 and 6 weeks of age. The thick muscle is the olive felt in the epigastrium, and visible peristaltic waves may cross the upper abdomen. Risk is higher in first-born boys and after macrolide exposure, especially erythromycin given in the first 2 weeks of life.
whyNot: Correct.
Failed recanalization causes atresia, which blocks the gut completely and causes vomiting from the first feeds.
Midgut volvulus with malrotation causes sudden bilious vomiting because the twist is below the papilla. It does not produce an olive-shaped mass.
Peptic scarring of the pylorus is a cause of gastric outlet obstruction in adults with chronic ulcer disease. It does not occur at this age.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely in this infant?
options: Chloride low, potassium high, bicarbonate low
Chloride normal, potassium high, bicarbonate high
Chloride low, potassium low, bicarbonate high
Chloride high, potassium low, bicarbonate low
approach: Note that the vomitus is pure gastric juice: HCl.
Losing H+ leaves bicarbonate behind, and losing Cl- lowers serum chloride.
Volume loss raises aldosterone, and bicarbonate in the urine carries K+ out, so potassium falls.
questions.why: Each parietal cell that secretes H+ into the lumen returns an equal amount of bicarbonate to the blood. Normally that bicarbonate is neutralized when acid enters the duodenum, but vomiting removes the acid so bicarbonate stays in the blood, causing metabolic alkalosis. Chloride is lost with the acid. Volume depletion activates aldosterone, which saves sodium at the cost of potassium and H+, so the kidney wastes potassium and keeps the alkalosis going. The result is hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, corrected with saline and potassium before surgery.
whyNot: High potassium with metabolic acidosis suggests renal failure or adrenal insufficiency, such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia with salt wasting.
Vomiting gastric juice always lowers chloride, and potassium falls through renal losses. Neither stays normal or rises.
Correct.
High chloride, low potassium, and low bicarbonate is a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, the pattern of diarrhea, which loses intestinal bicarbonate.

questions.stem: His vomitus contains no bile because bile enters the gut distal to the obstruction. In which part of the duodenum does bile normally enter?
options: Fourth (ascending) part
Second (descending) part
First (superior) part
Third (horizontal, inferior) part
approach: Connect nonbilious vomiting to an obstruction proximal to the bile entry point.
Recall where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct open.
The major duodenal papilla is on the posteromedial wall of the second part.
questions.why: The duodenum has four parts: superior, descending, horizontal, and ascending. The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct join at the hepatopancreatic ampulla and open at the major duodenal papilla in the second, descending part. Any block above this point, such as a thick pylorus, leaves vomitus free of bile. A block below it, such as midgut volvulus or most duodenal atresias, causes bilious vomiting. This is a key bedside sign for sorting neonatal obstruction.
whyNot: The fourth part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure at the ligament of Treitz. It also lies beyond the papilla.
Correct.
The first part, including the duodenal bulb, lies before the papilla. Bile does not enter here.
The third part crosses in front of the aorta and behind the superior mesenteric vessels. It lies beyond the papilla, and obstruction here causes bilious vomiting.

questions.stem: The thickened muscle in this condition has reduced neuronal nitric oxide synthase in the enteric nerve plexus that controls this muscle. Which of the following identifies this plexus and its location?
options: Submucosal plexus within the submucosa
Myenteric plexus within the submucosa
Submucosal plexus within the muscularis externa
Myenteric plexus within the muscularis externa
approach: Identify the thickened layer: circular smooth muscle, part of the muscularis externa.
Recall which plexus sits between the circular and longitudinal muscle.
That is the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, which controls motility.
questions.why: The gut wall has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa or adventitia. The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies in the submucosa and regulates secretion and blood flow. The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa and controls motility. Its nitrergic neurons normally relax the pylorus, and reduced nitric oxide signaling there has been described in pyloric stenosis.
whyNot: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies in the submucosa and controls secretion and local blood flow. The thickened layer here is the muscle coat.
The myenteric plexus does not sit in the submucosa. It lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
The submucosal plexus is not located in the muscularis externa.
Correct.

case: A 6-week-old girl is brought to the physician because of yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae since 2 weeks of age and pale gray stools. She was born at term and is breastfed. She is gaining weight. The liver edge is firm and palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin. Serum total bilirubin is 8.4 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.0), with direct bilirubin of 6.9 mg/dL (under 0.3). A hepatobiliary scan shows uptake of tracer by the liver but no excretion into the intestine after 24 hours. An intraoperative cholangiogram shows obliterated extrahepatic bile ducts. Diagnosis: biliary atresia.

questions.stem: Without surgical drainage of bile, which of the following is the most likely outcome for this infant?
options: Spontaneous reopening of the bile ducts by age 1 year
Kernicterus from bilirubin deposition in basal ganglia
Resolution of jaundice once breastfeeding is stopped
Biliary cirrhosis within the first years of life
approach: Recognize biliary atresia as progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic ducts.
Bile backs up into the liver, injuring ducts and hepatocytes.
Ongoing injury causes fibrosis and biliary cirrhosis.
questions.why: Biliary atresia is a progressive, inflammatory destruction of the extrahepatic bile ducts in the first weeks of life. Bile cannot leave the liver, so conjugated bilirubin rises, stools lose their color, and bile acids injure the liver. Portal fibrosis and bile duct proliferation progress to biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension, often within the first 1 to 2 years without treatment. A Kasai procedure works best when done early, and biliary atresia is the most common reason for liver transplantation in children.
whyNot: The obliteration in biliary atresia is progressive and does not reverse. Without a hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai procedure) or transplant, the damage continues.
Kernicterus is caused by unconjugated bilirubin, which is lipid soluble and crosses the blood-brain barrier. Her bilirubin is mostly conjugated.
Breast milk jaundice is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a well infant with normal stools. It does not cause conjugated jaundice with acholic stools.
Correct.

questions.stem: The obliterated ducts develop from which of the following embryonic structures?
options: Vitelline duct of the midgut endoderm
Hepatic diverticulum of foregut endoderm
Septum transversum splanchnic mesoderm
Dorsal pancreatic bud of the foregut endoderm
approach: Recall that the liver and biliary tree bud from the foregut in week 4.
The hepatic diverticulum gives liver cords and, through its stalk, the bile ducts.
Its cystic part forms the gallbladder and cystic duct.
questions.why: In week 4, the hepatic diverticulum grows from the endoderm of the distal foregut into the septum transversum. Its cranial part forms hepatocytes and intrahepatic ducts, while its caudal cystic part forms the gallbladder and cystic duct. The stalk connecting it to the duodenum becomes the common bile duct. The ventral pancreatic bud also arises near this stalk and rotates behind the duodenum, which explains annular pancreas when it migrates abnormally.
whyNot: The vitelline duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac and normally disappears. A remnant forms a Meckel diverticulum.
Correct.
The septum transversum gives rise to the connective tissue of the liver and the central tendon of the diaphragm. It does not form duct epithelium.
The dorsal pancreatic bud forms most of the pancreas, including the accessory duct. The bile ducts arise from the hepatic diverticulum.

questions.stem: Which of the following urine findings is most likely in this infant?
options: Bilirubin present, urobilinogen absent
Bilirubin absent, urobilinogen increased
Bilirubin present, urobilinogen increased
Bilirubin absent, urobilinogen absent
approach: Note the conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and passes into urine.
Note the acholic stools: no bile reaches the gut.
Without bilirubin in the gut, bacteria make no urobilinogen to reabsorb and excrete.
questions.why: Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and loosely bound to albumin, so when it builds up in blood it is filtered into the urine, making it dark. Urobilinogen is made by gut bacteria from bilirubin that reaches the intestine, and some of it is reabsorbed and excreted in urine. With complete obstruction, no bilirubin reaches the gut, so urobilinogen disappears from urine and the stools turn pale. Hemolysis shows the opposite pattern: unconjugated bilirubin that cannot enter urine, and high urine urobilinogen.
whyNot: Correct.
Absent urine bilirubin with high urobilinogen is the pattern of hemolysis. The excess bilirubin is unconjugated, which cannot pass into urine.
Bilirubin and urobilinogen can both be raised in some hepatocellular injury, but urobilinogen needs bile to reach the gut. Her ducts are blocked.
Her conjugated bilirubin is high and water soluble, so it spills into the urine. Urine bilirubin cannot be absent.

questions.stem: Surgery is delayed. At 9 weeks of age, she bleeds for a long time from a heel-stick site. Prothrombin time is 24 seconds (11 to 14) and corrects within 24 hours after a parenteral dose of vitamin K. Which of the following best explains the prolonged prothrombin time?
options: Consumption of clotting factors in widespread microthrombi
An inhibitory antibody against coagulation factor VIII
Poor vitamin K absorption without bile acid micelles
Reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factor proteins
approach: Note the fix: parenteral vitamin K corrects the prothrombin time.
Recall that vitamin K is fat soluble and needs bile acid micelles to be absorbed.
Without bile in the gut, vitamin K deficiency develops, and factors II, VII, IX, and X are not carboxylated.
questions.why: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat soluble and are absorbed within bile acid micelles. With no bile reaching the gut, they are poorly absorbed. Vitamin K is needed for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S, so deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time and causes bleeding. Parenteral vitamin K bypasses the gut, which is why the clotting test corrects. Over time she is also at risk for night blindness, rickets, and vitamin E neuropathy and hemolysis.
whyNot: Disseminated intravascular coagulation uses up factors and platelets, usually in a severely ill patient. Vitamin K would not correct it.
A factor VIII inhibitor prolongs the partial thromboplastin time and leaves the prothrombin time normal. Vitamin K does not affect it.
Correct.
Hepatocyte failure lowers clotting factor production, but that does not correct with vitamin K. The quick correction shows the liver can still make the factors.

dx: Omphalocele with cleft lip and palate in trisomy 13
case: A newborn boy is examined shortly after birth at 38 weeks' gestation. Prenatal ultrasonography showed an abdominal wall defect and a single fused forebrain consistent with holoprosencephaly. He has a midline abdominal wall defect about 5 cm wide at the base of the umbilical cord, through which loops of small bowel and part of the liver protrude. He also has a bilateral cleft lip with a cleft palate, small eyes, and an extra digit on each hand. Karyotype is 47,XY,+13. Diagnosis: omphalocele with cleft lip and palate in a newborn with trisomy 13.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes his abdominal wall defect, as compared with gastroschisis?
options: Viscera covered by intact skin protruding through a weak umbilical ring
Exposed bladder mucosa through a defect in the lower abdominal wall
Viscera in a sac of peritoneum and amnion, with the cord on the sac
Uncovered viscera passing through a full-thickness defect right of the cord
approach: Note the defect is midline at the base of the cord and contains liver.
Recall that an omphalocele keeps a membrane covering, while gastroschisis does not.
Link the trisomy to omphalocele, which is often associated with chromosomal anomalies.
questions.why: An omphalocele is a midline defect at the umbilical ring through which viscera protrude inside a sac of peritoneum and amnion, with the umbilical cord inserting on the sac. It is often linked to trisomy 13 or 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and heart defects. Gastroschisis is a defect beside the cord, usually on the right, with uncovered bowel that floats in amniotic fluid and becomes thick and matted. Gastroschisis is rarely associated with other anomalies, but it carries a risk of intestinal atresia.
whyNot: A skin-covered bulge at the umbilicus is an umbilical hernia, common in infants and usually closing by itself.
Exposed bladder mucosa in the lower abdominal wall is bladder exstrophy, a defect of the infraumbilical body wall and cloacal membrane.
Correct.
Uncovered bowel beside a normally inserted cord, usually to the right, is gastroschisis. It is seldom linked to trisomies.

questions.stem: He has trouble feeding, and milk comes out of his nose when he tries to suck. Failure of fusion of which of the following structures most directly explains this problem?
options: Lateral palatine shelves
Maxillary and medial nasal prominences
Maxillary and mandibular prominences
Two medial nasal prominences
approach: Note the symptom: milk passes from mouth to nose, so the oral and nasal cavities connect.
The roof of the mouth is the secondary palate.
The secondary palate forms from fusion of the two lateral palatine shelves.
questions.why: The upper lip forms when each maxillary prominence fuses with the merged medial nasal prominences; failure gives cleft lip. The secondary palate forms when the lateral palatine shelves grow up above the tongue and fuse with each other and the nasal septum; failure gives cleft palate. With a cleft palate, the infant cannot seal the oral cavity to make suction, and milk passes into the nose. Cleft lip and palate are common in trisomy 13, often with holoprosencephaly.
whyNot: Correct.
Failure of the maxillary and medial nasal prominences to fuse produces cleft lip. A cleft lip alone does not open the mouth into the nasal cavity behind the gums.
Failure of the maxillary and mandibular prominences to merge widens the mouth (macrostomia). It does not create an opening into the nose.

The two medial nasal prominences fuse to form the intermaxillary segment, including the philtrum and primary palate. A failure here causes a median cleft lip, which is rare and does not explain nasal regurgitation.

questions.stem: Failure of which of the following normal developmental events most directly explains the bowel loops within the defect?
options: Rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery
Obliteration of the vitelline duct
Recanalization of the intestinal lumen
Return of the herniated midgut loop
approach: Recall that the midgut normally herniates into the umbilical cord in week 6.
It rotates and normally returns to the abdomen by week 10.
If it fails to return, the bowel stays in a sac at the umbilicus: an omphalocele.
questions.why: In week 6, the midgut grows faster than the abdominal cavity and herniates into the umbilical cord. While outside, it rotates 90 degrees counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, and it completes 270 degrees as it returns to the abdomen around week 10. If the bowel does not return, it remains outside within the cord covering, forming an omphalocele. A large omphalocele that contains liver also reflects failure of the lateral body folds to close the abdominal wall. Malrotation often coexists.
whyNot: Failed or incomplete rotation is malrotation, which leaves the bowel inside the abdomen in an abnormal position with Ladd bands and a risk of volvulus.
A persistent vitelline duct remnant causes a Meckel diverticulum or an umbilical fistula draining ileal contents. It does not leave bowel loops outside the abdominal wall.
Failed recanalization causes atresia or stenosis of the gut lumen. It does not move bowel outside the abdomen.
Correct.

questions.stem: After repair of his defects, a swallow study is performed. As he swallows, the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes before the bolus arrives. Which of the following mediates this relaxation?
options: Circulating gastrin from antral G cells
Vagal neurons releasing nitric oxide and VIP
Vagal neurons releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
Sympathetic neurons releasing norepinephrine
approach: Note that the sphincter opens before the bolus arrives, so the signal must be neural.
Recall that the vagus carries both excitatory and inhibitory fibers to the sphincter.
Inhibitory fibers act through myenteric neurons that release nitric oxide and VIP.
questions.why: The lower esophageal sphincter is tonically contracted at rest to block reflux. When a swallow begins, the medullary swallowing center sends signals down the vagus to inhibitory myenteric neurons. These release nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide, which relax the sphincter and the proximal stomach before the bolus arrives. In achalasia, these inhibitory neurons are lost, so the sphincter fails to relax.
whyNot: Gastrin raises lower esophageal sphincter tone if anything. It does not relax the sphincter during a swallow.
Correct.
Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors contracts the sphincter muscle and maintains its tone between swallows.
Sympathetic input has only a minor role in the lower esophageal sphincter and does not produce swallow-induced relaxation.

dx: Acute mesenteric ischemia from an atrial fibrillation embolus
case: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 4 hours after the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain around the umbilicus, followed by one episode of vomiting and a loose stool. She has atrial fibrillation and stopped taking her anticoagulant 1 month ago. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 118/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg. She is writhing in pain, but the abdomen is soft and only mildly tender without guarding. Serum lactate is 5.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). CT angiography shows an embolus in the superior mesenteric artery distal to its origin. Diagnosis: acute mesenteric ischemia from an embolus.

questions.stem: Which of the following histories, if present instead, would most suggest chronic mesenteric ischemia?
options: Crampy lower abdominal pain relieved by defecation
Pain after meals, fear of eating, and weight loss
Sudden severe pain beginning shortly after cardioversion
Painful bloody diarrhea after an episode of shock
approach: Recall that chronic mesenteric ischemia comes from atherosclerosis of several mesenteric arteries.
Flow is enough at rest but not after meals, when gut demand rises.
Look for pain after eating, food fear, and weight loss: intestinal angina.
questions.why: Chronic mesenteric ischemia is usually caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of two or more of the celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries. After a meal, blood flow to the gut must rise, and when it cannot, the patient has pain 15 to 60 minutes after eating. Patients learn to avoid food and lose weight. Acute mesenteric ischemia, as in this patient, is most often an embolus from atrial fibrillation to the superior mesenteric artery, with severe pain out of proportion to the exam and a rising lactate.
whyNot: Crampy pain relieved by defecation, with no alarm features, suggests irritable bowel syndrome, a functional disorder without ischemia.
Correct.
Sudden pain soon after cardioversion suggests an embolus dislodged from the left atrium, which is acute mesenteric ischemia like hers.
Painful bloody diarrhea after low blood pressure suggests ischemic colitis at a watershed area of the colon, such as the splenic flexure.

questions.stem: At laparotomy, the segments supplied by the occluded artery are dusky. Which of the following segments is most likely to remain well perfused?
options: Terminal ileum
Ascending colon
Cecum and appendix
Descending colon
approach: Identify the occluded vessel: the superior mesenteric artery.
Recall its territory: distal duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.
Choose the segment in the inferior mesenteric territory.
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, from the distal duodenum through the jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and about the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut, from the distal transverse colon to the upper rectum, including the descending colon. Emboli often lodge beyond the first jejunal or middle colic branches, so the proximal jejunum may be spared. The marginal artery links the two territories, but its weakest points at the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction are prone to ischemic colitis after hypotension.
whyNot: The terminal ileum is supplied by the ileocolic and ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery. It is at high risk.
The ascending colon is supplied by the right colic and ileocolic branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
The cecum and appendix are supplied by the ileocolic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her pain was first felt around the umbilicus?
options: Intercostal nerves in the parietal peritoneum near the umbilicus are irritated
Hindgut visceral afferents enter the cord at T10, the segment of umbilical skin
Midgut visceral afferents enter the cord at T10, the segment of umbilical skin
Foregut visceral afferents enter the cord at T10, the segment of umbilical skin
approach: Identify the ischemic bowel as a midgut derivative.
Recall that visceral pain is poorly localized and referred by embryologic origin.
Midgut pain is referred to the periumbilical region, the T10 dermatome.
questions.why: Visceral pain fibers from the gut travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at the segments that supplied the gut tube in the embryo. The brain cannot localize this input well and refers it to the skin served by the same segments. Foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium, midgut pain around the umbilicus at about T10, and hindgut pain in the suprapubic region. Pain becomes sharp and localized only when the parietal peritoneum is inflamed, which is why early mesenteric ischemia causes severe pain with a soft abdomen.
whyNot: Irritation of the parietal peritoneum gives sharp, well-localized pain over the diseased organ with guarding. Her soft abdomen shows the peritoneum is not yet involved.
Hindgut visceral pain, as from the sigmoid colon, enters lower segments and is referred to the suprapubic region.
Correct.
Foregut visceral pain, as from the stomach or duodenum, enters higher thoracic segments and is referred to the epigastrium.

questions.stem: She undergoes embolectomy and resection of a short ileal segment and has no caloric intake for the next 3 days. On the third day, which of the following is the main source of her blood glucose?
options: Hepatic gluconeogenesis from amino acids, lactate, and glycerol
Hepatic glycogenolysis releasing glucose from stored glycogen
Muscle glycogenolysis releasing free glucose into the blood
Hepatic conversion of circulating ketone bodies into new glucose
approach: Note the timing: 3 days without food.
Liver glycogen lasts about a day, so after that the liver must make new glucose.
Gluconeogenesis uses alanine and other amino acids from muscle, lactate, and glycerol from fat.
questions.why: In the first hours of fasting, the liver keeps blood glucose up by breaking down its glycogen. Those stores are largely gone after about 24 to 48 hours. The liver then relies on gluconeogenesis, using alanine and other amino acids from muscle protein, lactate from red cells and muscle (the Cori cycle), and glycerol released from fat. At the same time, fatty acid oxidation feeds hepatic ketogenesis. The liver exports ketones to the brain and muscle but cannot use them, because it lacks the enzyme succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase).
whyNot: Correct.
Liver glycogen is the main source in the first 12 to 24 hours of fasting, but it is largely used up within about 1 to 2 days.
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen supplies glucose only to the muscle itself. It cannot release free glucose into the blood.
Ketone bodies come from acetyl-CoA and cannot be converted into glucose. The brain uses them in place of glucose as fasting continues.
